steps.observation: Work on this for 300 seconds; do not stop early. Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
On the rugged coast of Maine, where the Atlantic Ocean crashes against jagged cliffs, stood the venerable Windward Light. It was a tall, solemn structure with a rich history of keeping ships safe from the treacherous rocks below. For nearly thirty years, Michael Harrington had served as its steadfast keeper, a solitary yet fulfilling existence.

Michael was a man of few words, preferring the company of the sea and the reliable pulse of the Fresnel lens over the unpredictable cacophony of human interaction. His days were shaped by routine: tending to the light, performing maintenance on the building, and preparing hearty meals in the tiny kitchen.

Yet, there were moments when the silence of the lighthouse was broken by visitors from the nearby town of Seabrook. They would come with stories and local news, bringing with them the warmth of the world beyond. But when the storms rolled in, as they often did, Michael was alone with the wind and rain as his companions.

One autumn afternoon, as the sea was calm and the sky a crisp blue, Michael received an unexpected letter delivered by a local boy from town. The envelope was from the Harbor Authority, informing him that the lighthouse would soon be automated, rendering his position obsolete. In a few short months, machines would take over his duties; the light would switch on and off and keep its watch without human hands.

At first, Michael felt adrift, like a ship untethered from its moorings. Windward Light had become not just his workplace, but his home, his sanctuary. Without it, he wondered how he would find purpose.

Over the following weeks, as autumn began to yield to the icy grip of winter, Michael tried to embrace the inevitable change. He spent his days capturing the moments of his time at the lighthouse through sketches and paintings. The view from the top, the intricate mechanism of the lamp, the sweeping coastal vistas—each was immortalized on canvas.

One day, as the first snowflakes began to fall and the sky took on a leaden hue, a girl appeared at the base of the lighthouse. Her name was Claire, and she was fascinated by the lighthouse, having spent many summers with her grandmother in Seabrook.

“I’ve always wanted to see inside,” she said, her eyes wide with wonder.

Michael smiled and invited her in. He gave her a tour, explaining the intricacies of the machinery and the dedication it took to keep the light shining.

“But it won’t be the same,” Claire said, her voice tinged with sadness, when Michael explained the upcoming automation.

Michael nodded, sharing her sentiment. Yet, in showing Claire the magical world within the lighthouse, he felt a small ember of hope—perhaps the spirit of the place would live on in those who had cherished it.

As Michael prepared for his departure, he donated many of his paintings to the town's local museum, hoping they would inspire future generations to appreciate the lighthouse and the life of its keepers.

On his last night at Windward Light, Michael climbed to the lantern room. The storm had come, as if to give him a grand send-off, with waves battering the cliffs and the wind howling through every crevice of the structure.

He watched the beam of light sweep across the dark, storm-tossed ocean, and for a moment, he saw himself reflected in its path. Tomorrow, he would leave, but the light would remain, a constant in an ever-changing world.

Michael took a final walk along the lantern room, touching the glass with reverence. It was time to go, to let the future take hold.

Dawn broke with a serene pink glow, and Michael headed toward the mainland, his heart heavy but his steps steady. As he glanced back one last time, he knew that Windward Light would continue its vigil, as steadfast as ever, its legacy carried by those it had touched. And somewhere within him, like a flame refusing to be extinguished, was the enduring brightness of his years as a lighthouse keeper.
